name: German Volume Training

lead: German Volume Training (GVT) is a bodybuilding method built around a single exercise performed for 10 sets of 10 repetitions with a moderate load and short rests. Lifters use it to add muscle mass, which changes how the shoulders, chest, arms and legs fill out a frame.

The idea is that very high volume on one movement gives the muscle a large amount of work in one session. A handful of small trials have compared the 10-set approach with 5 sets of 10 and measured lean mass and strength; these are described below.

paras: Practitioners typically pick one major compound lift per muscle group, use roughly 60 percent of their one-repetition maximum, rest about 60 to 90 seconds between sets and split the week by body part. Accessory work is added after the main 10x10 block. Programs usually run for several weeks before changing.

The main reported issues are heavy fatigue, intense soreness and longer recovery, plus the usual injury risks of high-volume lifting. Lifters often mention using a spotter on bench pressing. People with blood pressure or heart conditions are generally advised by clinicians to discuss any intense training with a doctor.

chain: Ten sets of ten reps on one lift
High training volume for the target muscle
angle.text: Lifters use GVT as a hypertrophy block to add size to a lagging muscle group. The look it aims for is greater muscle size in the chest, arms, shoulders and legs, produced by the training stimulus together with food and recovery.

lead: German Volume Training (GVT), also called the 10x10 or 10 sets method, is a resistance-training scheme in which one exercise is performed for ten sets of ten repetitions, typically at about 60 percent of a lifter's one-repetition maximum with 60 to 90 seconds of rest between sets.[1][2] It is widely described as a bodybuilding method for gaining muscle mass quickly.[2]

People use it to look more muscular: more lean mass in the chest, back, arms and legs is the visible payoff of the approach, and the extreme volume is meant to drive muscle growth in the targeted area. Trainees commonly run it as a body-part split and pair it with extra assisted or accessory exercises.[2]

Research on GVT is small. A 2017 randomized trial of 19 men compared 6 weeks of 10 sets versus 5 sets of 10 repetitions and found lean mass gains in both groups, with trunk and arm lean mass favouring the 5-set group.[3] A 12-week pilot study reported no additional benefit from the 10-set group.[4] Other studies have used GVT as a fatiguing test protocol for supplements and for dieting bodybuilders.[5][6][7]

paras: GVT centres on one main exercise per muscle group, performed for ten consecutive sets of ten repetitions. Because the load is moderate relative to a lifter's maximum, the early sets feel manageable and the later ones become hard as fatigue accumulates.[2] A weekly structure usually assigns a different muscle group to each training day, with complementary groups sometimes paired in one session.[2]

Grokipedia describes the method as having been used for decades by weightlifters and ties its spread to later coaches and bodybuilding media.[1] The English Wikipedia page cites a bodybuilding article by coach Charles Poliquin as its source for the method.[2]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting culture
paras: On T Nation, GVT is mentioned in training logs and confession-style threads, where members describe discovering it, finding it demanding and noting that bench work calls for a spotter.[8] Users frame it as a way to bring up a stubborn body part and to change a routine after plateaus.

A randomized trial by Amirthalingam and colleagues assigned 19 healthy men to 6 weeks of 10 or 5 sets of 10 repetitions, three sessions per week. Both groups increased lean body mass; trunk and arm lean mass gains favoured the 5-set group, and leg lean mass and muscle thickness did not change significantly across groups.[3]

The same group's 12-week pilot study with 12 men found no significant changes in total, trunk or arm lean mass, and an observed decrease in leg lean mass in the 10-set group between weeks 6 and 12. The authors concluded that more than 5 sets per exercise did not produce greater strength or hypertrophy in that sample.[4]

Other trials used GVT as a standard fatiguing workout. In two randomized trials, citrulline malate did not change performance in a GVT session in trained participants.[5][6] In a trial of competition bodybuilders on energy restriction, researchers assessed GVT performance after a carbohydrate refeed.[7] A crossover study of a single GVT session reported lower blood pressure after exercise along with higher heart rate and perceived exertion.[9]

Reported downsides are marked soreness, long recovery and fatigue.[2] The acute-response study recorded a rise in heart rate and rating of perceived exertion after a single session.[9] Forum users recommend a spotter for heavy pressing sets.[8]

lore.intro: Lifters on T Nation treat GVT as a classic high-volume routine to try for size or to break a plateau.[8]
